body: Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands belongs in this calendar for more than an anniversary. Its history brings cooperation and division of roles into direct contact with tactical layer and planning, and recognizable elements such as Sync Shot, Bolivia make that relationship concrete. In 2017, those choices connected rules, presentation and player memory instead of treating technology and storytelling as separate tracks. The historical interest lies in the practical decisions that turned an ambition into something people could play, read and remember. The chapters that follow move from specific systems and production choices to their consequences, tracing how Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands established its identity and why parts of that identity continued to matter afterward.

NieR: Automata is born from the meeting of Yoko Taro's direction and PlatinumGames' action expertise. The studio's official website presents it as an open-world action RPG running at 60 frames per second, but that speed does not remove character progression. Weapons, levels, quests and configurations intertwine with dodges, combos and the Pod's ranged attacks. PlatinumGames works to keep the time between input and response readable, even tuning the exact moment when one animation can be cancelled into another. The result avoids separating two audiences: players seeking precision in the action can study timing and combinations, while those who favor progression can adjust equipment and difficulty. Fluidity therefore becomes a bridge between the combat system and the role-playing structure.

The plug-in chip system treats the android as a configurable machine. Some chips alter statistics and combat abilities, others add interface functions, and the player must distribute a limited amount of space among different advantages. In an interview published by PlayStation, Takahisa Taura and Yoko Taro explain how this solution makes it possible to blend action and RPG systems without relying only on traditional equipment. The most radical choice is that even seemingly indispensable HUD elements can be treated as components installed in the body. The menu therefore stops being a layer outside the fiction. Customizing 2B means deciding which information and automations deserve memory. It is a solution consistent with android protagonists and makes one of the game's recurring questions visible: where does identity end and assigned function begin?

NieR: Automata does not use endings only as final rewards. Before release, Yoko Taro explained that anyone who stops at the first ending has not seen even half of the story. Later routes revisit events the player has already experienced, but change the character, the available information and access to parts of the system. Repetition therefore does not exist simply to extend the running time: it changes the meaning of what the player remembers. A battle seen through 2B can take on a different interpretation when 9S introduces hacking, dialogue and different knowledge. The game builds its narrative on top of a memory that has already formed, then forces that memory to be reconsidered. The method is especially effective because the player is not simply given a corrective flashback. They must return to the same places and perform new actions to discover how incomplete the first interpretation was.

The Earth of NieR: Automata alternates between urban ruins, deserts, forests and industrial structures, but its narrative density does not depend only on the main plot. Before release, PlayStation presented hubs and side quests as an important part of the RPG structure, giving 2B and the other androids assignments that expand their relationship with the Resistance and the machines. These detours matter because they bring the game's themes to the surface through smaller situations: rituals, work, memory, fear and imitation do not belong only to the major revelations. The open world therefore works as a space in which behaviors are compared. A machine encountered far from the main objective can raise a question that remains active during later events. Exploration is not only a way to gather resources; it slowly builds the emotional vocabulary through which the player will interpret the war.

Keiichi Okabe explained that for NieR: Automata he sought a more dynamic sound than in the first NieR, one suited to the science-fiction setting while preserving the voices and melancholy that defined the series. The result supports a game capable of moving quickly from exploration to combat and from quiet to tragedy. The music must not only accompany a scene, but preserve its identity when the pace changes. Okabe has described sometimes beginning with the beat for battle tracks and, in other cases, with a melody imagined as a voice. This flexibility fits the structure of the work, where the same places can be revisited several times and take on different meanings. The soundtrack thus becomes a parallel memory: recognizing a theme means remembering a space, a character and an emotional state at the same time.

Behind the fluidity of NieR: Automata is technical work that PlatinumGames showed during development. Takahisa Taura describes test levels used to check animations and effects, together with tools that precisely control when a movement can be interrupted and linked to the next one. It is a less spectacular side of production, but it helps explain why 2B responds continuously even when the player alternates attacks, dodges and weapons. The collaboration with Yoko Taro is therefore not a matter of placing a story on top of an action system that was already complete. It requires the character's behavior to support the tone and rhythm of the work. Animation technology becomes a form of direction: it determines how long a gesture remains visible, when it can be corrected and how much control the player perceives during a fast sequence.

Burnout Revenge changes an instinctive rule of racing games: not all traffic has to be avoided. Criterion introduces traffic checking, which lets the player hit many vehicles travelling in the same direction and use them as projectiles against rivals or other cars. The studio still recalls the idea today through Traffic Attack, a mode built around knocking cars off the road. The consequence is perceptual before it is competitive. A crowded lane, normally read as a danger, can become a resource if the player recognizes which vehicles are safe to hit and the direction in which they will be pushed. The system still preserves a hierarchy: buses, heavy trucks and oncoming traffic remain threats. Speed therefore comes from the ability to distinguish, within a few moments, what must be avoided from what can be turned into an advantage.

The word Revenge in the title is not merely an aggressive tone. Criterion builds progression around rivalry and gives greater importance to taking down the opponent who has already sent the player into a wall. In interviews from the period, the team explained that a Revenge Takedown was meant to carry more weight than an ordinary takedown, encouraging the player to recognize and pursue a specific opponent. This choice changes the way a crowded race is read. The rival is no longer just a car occupying a position in the standings: it retains a small history of the previous interaction. Aggression therefore becomes memory. Even when a race lasts only a few minutes, the system builds a relationship simple enough to be recognized at speed. Burnout Revenge uses personal conflict to give shape to a game that might otherwise become an indistinct sequence of spectacular crashes.

The Xbox 360 edition released in North America on March 7, 2006 is not simply a high-definition port. Criterion uses it above all to push online play, introducing Live Revenge and Save & Share. The first feature records persistent rivalries between users and highlights who has already defeated whom; the second lets players cut moments from replays, save them and share them with others. In a racing game built on unpredictable crashes, this possibility turns private spectacle into a social object. A successful takedown does not end when the race is over: it can become a clip to show, rate and remember. Looking back, the studio connects these ideas with social features it developed later in other Criterion games. The new console is therefore used not only for greater graphical detail, but to extend the life of the event after the impact.

I Am Alive turns climbing into continuous stamina management. Ubisoft presented the system as one of the cores of survival: scaling ruined buildings makes it possible to reach breathable air and resources, but every handhold consumes energy and forces the player to judge distance, grips and opportunities to rest. Height is therefore not merely panoramic spectacle. It becomes a cost that can leave the protagonist with no margin at the worst possible moment. The post-catastrophe city is read vertically, in search of routes that combine safety with potential reward. This also makes stopping meaningful. Before climbing, the player studies the facade and tries to understand whether there is enough stamina to complete the route. Survival comes from a simple but readable measure: every meter gained moves the player farther from the ground and closer to exhaustion.

Combat in I Am Alive avoids treating ammunition as an abundant resource. Ubisoft describes an intimidation system in which some enemies may back away from a weapon even when the magazine is empty, while more determined opponents can call the bluff. The tension therefore comes from incomplete information. The player knows how many bullets they have; the person in front of them does not. Aiming the weapon becomes a social decision before it is a ballistic one, because it can stop a confrontation without consuming a resource or make the situation worse if the threat is not believed. This mechanic makes the value of scarcity visible. A bullet is worth more than the damage it causes: it represents credibility, control of space and future possibility. Violence can be effective precisely when it is not carried out, as long as the opponent believes that it could be.

The Haventon of I Am Alive is built around the consequences of a cataclysm that left buildings destroyed and streets submerged in toxic dust. Xbox describes a protagonist forced to seek breathable air by climbing toward the upper parts of buildings, while Ubisoft links this exposure to the management of stamina and resources. The post-apocalyptic landscape therefore does not function only as atmosphere. It establishes a vertical hierarchy: descending can offer supplies, but means accepting a more hostile environment; climbing consumes energy, but makes it possible to breathe and get oriented. On March 7, 2012, the game arrives on Xbox Live Arcade as a compact digital experience, and this structure concentrates survival around a few very clear systems. The environment does not need an abstract danger bar: dust, height and breathing directly communicate when the player is spending too much.
